item.research_question: Does hydrogen exposure cause catastrophic failure (hydrogen embrittlement) or can it improve mechanical properties in an equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy?
item.processing_route: Vacuum induction melting of pure elements (Co20Cr20Fe20Mn20Ni20 at.%), hot-rolling at 900 °C (50% reduction), homogenization at 1200 °C for 2 h, water-quenching, cold-rolling (60% reduction), and annealing at 900 °C for 3 min followed by water-quenching.
item.test_conditions: Electrochemical hydrogen charging in 0.1 M NaOH + 0.05 g·L−1 CH4N2S at pH = 13 and 25 °C; pre-charging durations of 12 h (15 mA·cm−2), 72 h (25 mA·cm−2), and 240 h (100 mA·cm−2); in-situ tensile testing at a rate of 1 × 10−4 S−1 with continuous charging.
key_findings: The hydrogen-free alloy exhibited an ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of 545 MPa and total elongation of ~68%.
Pre-charging for 12 h at 15 mA·cm−2 (8.01 wt.ppm H) increased UTS to 571 MPa and uniform elongation to ~71%.
Pre-charging for 72 h at 25 mA·cm−2 (15.22 wt.ppm H) increased UTS to 588 MPa and uniform elongation to ~71%, representing ~7.9% and ~4.4% increases over the hydrogen-free sample.
Pre-charging for 240 h at 100 mA·cm−2 (33.25 wt.ppm H) showed a slightly reduced increment in strength and ductility compared to the 15.22 wt.ppm sample, suggesting saturation.
Hydrogen alloying did not exert significant effects on the yield strength of the alloy.
The hydrogen alloyed HEA with 15.22 wt.ppm H exhibited the highest strain-hardening rate among all conditions.
The density of deformation nanotwins significantly increased in hydrogen alloyed samples compared to the hydrogen-free alloy.
The intrinsic stacking fault energy of the alloy is ~19 mJ·m2, which is reduced further by hydrogen.
item.mechanism: Hydrogen reduces the stacking fault energy and phase stability of the f.c.c. lattice, which triggers more intense nanotwinning upon loading. This increased nanotwin density enhances the work-hardening rate via the 'dynamic Hall-Petch' effect (continuous grain fragmentation and reduced dislocation mean free path), thereby simultaneously increasing strength and ductility. At very high hydrogen concentrations, unfavorable mechanisms like hydrogen enhanced localized plasticity or surface cracking compete with the beneficial twinning, leading to saturation or slight reduction in gains.
item.limitations: The text notes that at the highest hydrogen concentration (33.25 wt.ppm), the increment in strength and ductility was reduced, likely due to a competition between beneficial nanotwining and unfavorable mechanisms like hydrogen enhanced localized plasticity or initial surface cracks caused by high surface hydrogen concentration.
item.future_work: The authors propose that these results open new pathways for the design of strong, ductile, and hydrogen tolerant materials by utilizing hydrogen to tune beneficial hardening mechanisms rather than viewing it solely as a harmful impurity.
quotes: hydrogen in an equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) leads not to catastrophic weakening, but instead increases both, its strength and ductility.
hydrogen alloying with a proper concentration actually jointly increases both strength and ductility.
